entities.summary: Cardinal Guillaume, Guillermo or William de Croÿ, a member of the noble House of Croÿ, was Prince-Bishop of Cambrai from 1516 to 1519 and Archbishop of Toledo from 1517 to 1521. He was born in the Habsburg Netherlands and died in Worms, Germany.

entities.name: William de Croÿ
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
William de Croÿ (1498–1521), born into the influential House of Croÿ in Flanders, ascended to the highest echelons of the Catholic Church at an extraordinarily young age, becoming Prince-Bishop of Cambrai at 18 and Archbishop of Toledo and a Cardinal at just 19. His meteoric rise was not due to spiritual merit but was a direct consequence of the political ambitions of his uncle, William de Croÿ, Lord of Chièvres, who served as the chief minister to the newly crowned King of Spain and future Holy Roman Emperor, Charles V. De Croÿ’s appointment to the primatial see of Toledo, bypassing Spanish candidates, symbolized Habsburg imperial imposition and became a flashpoint for Castilian resentment, directly contributing to the outbreak of the Comuneros Revolt.

His ecclesiastical career began with the Prince-Bishopric of Cambrai in 1516, a strategically important diocese within the Habsburg Netherlands. However, his most controversial appointment came in 1517 when, despite his youth and lack of ecclesiastical experience, he was named Archbishop of Toledo, the wealthiest and most powerful see in Spain. This appointment, along with his cardinalate bestowed by Pope Leo X, was a calculated move by Charles V and his Flemish advisors to secure control over the vast revenues and political influence of the Spanish Church. De Croÿ never resided in Toledo, instead governing through vicars, exacerbating the perception of foreign exploitation and fueling the burgeoning Castilian opposition to Charles V's rule.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: William de Croÿ's controversial appointment to the Archbishopric of Toledo at a young age, driven by Habsburg political ambition, became a key catalyst for the Comuneros Revolt, a major challenge to Charles V's early rule in Spain. His career exemplifies the entanglement of church and state power in early modern Europe and the tensions between imperial governance and local autonomy.
